title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
hook: he wanted to touch the wounds, and then said my Lord and my God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Emmaus: seven miles with a stranger, and bread broken at the end. Your line was was not our heart burning. What warmed you yesterday that you only noticed later? Day seventy.

Somebody in every group chat is the one who says, pics or it didn't happen. That's Thomas. On Easter night the risen Jesus comes to the disciples behind locked doors, and Thomas isn't there. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he doesn't believe a word. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." Not just see. Touch. For two thousand years he's been called doubting Thomas. Today: what actually happened eight days later.
screen: `PICS OR IT DIDN'T HAPPEN.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.` → `I WILL NOT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: First, who Thomas was. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward Jerusalem, where people had tried to stone him, it's Thomas who says: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." He's not a coward. He's blunt, and loyal, and he won't pretend. Eight days after Easter, they're together again, and this time Thomas is there. The doors are shut. Jesus stands in the middle and says, "Peace be to you." Then he turns to Thomas and offers him exactly what he asked for: put in your finger, see my hands, bring your hand, put it into my side, "and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't scold him for asking. He shows him the wounds. And here's the surprise: the Gospel never says Thomas touched them. What it gives us is his answer: "My Lord, and my God." Nobody in any of the Gospels says anything bigger about who Jesus is. The doubter makes the fullest confession of faith. Then Jesus adds a line for everyone after: "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." That means the listener, too. Catholics hear this Gospel every year on the Sunday after Easter. And there's an old Catholic custom: when the priest lifts the host at Mass, some people whisper Thomas's words. My Lord and my God. Tradition says Thomas later carried the faith all the way to India, and Christians there still call themselves Saint Thomas Christians. So that was the week: remember me, his mother stood, it is finished, Holy Saturday, the garden, Emmaus, and Thomas.
screen: `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE WITH HIM.` · `HE SHOWS HIM THE WOUNDS.` · `NO VERSE SAYS HE TOUCHED THEM.` · `THE DOUBTER'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `MY LORD, AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your honest doubt. Settle and breathe. Name one thing about faith, or God, or your own life, that you're not sure about. Don't hide it and don't force an answer. Just hold it in the open, the way Thomas said his out loud to his friends. If you pray, you can bring it to God as plainly as he did. Jesus, in the story, didn't turn him away. The bell holds the time.
Thomas. The disciple who wanted to see and touch, and who then said the biggest words in the Gospels: my Lord and my God. Today's word.
Your line: doubt can kneel too. Today, when someone admits they're not sure, don't rush to fix them. Honest questions have a place. Day seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Thomas every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some quietly say 'my Lord and my God' when the host is raised at Mass.

options: say, my Lord, and my God.
fork.reveal: John never says he touched. he gives us only the answer: "My Lord, and my God."

original.note: Greek form of an Aramaic name meaning twin. John also calls him Didymus, the Greek for twin.

trapdoor: what you thought: doubting Thomas, the one who didn't have enough faith.
what it means: the blunt, loyal disciple asks honestly, is shown the wounds, and says the fullest confession in the Gospels.
what a scholar hears: Thomas means twin, and John never says he touched. and tradition takes him to India, where Saint Thomas Christians still carry his name.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 20:25–29 and 11:16 given from memory; confirm.
'Nobody in any of the Gospels says anything bigger about who Jesus is': a common reading of 20:28 as the high point of John's Christology; Keeper may want it softened.
Custom of saying 'My Lord and my God' at the elevation: associated with an indulgence granted by Pius X (1907). Confirm.
John 20:19–31 is the Gospel of the Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy Sunday) in all three years of the lectionary. Confirm.
Thomas in India: tradition (Acts of Thomas; the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala); stated as tradition.
